chapter: New Orleans bands, Louis and the Lyric
title: Duplicated re-typing of pages 49-54
summary: This run repeats the text of the earlier pages almost word for word (Lovie Taylor, gambling, the Cadillac, Lee Collins, Robichaux and the Lyric) and ends Tape 1.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Jordan's band. And they played 'Sweet Georgia Brown' for a cat to dance by the name of Lovie Taylor. Boy and did that cat dance. And that music was so precious perfect behind this cat's taps. He was a tap dancer but it was soft shoe. He didn't have no taps on his shoes.
It's a more subtle thing really than straight tap.
Yes, oh boy and that music. And that cat was dancing right with that music. Do you remember that Marge?
Yes.
The music had to be soft.
Oh, very soft.
Well that's what we would do on our nights off.
And they were playing the melody so beautifully.
Because Zutto was never A gamble R.
Oh you didn't have that problem?
No. No, he didn't gamble. I was the gambler, but he......
Well that's very good because...... ......

But he liked the better things, in life. He liked the theater very, very much. And sports. He liked ball games. I never went to a baseball game in my life. I hated baseball. But after Zutty was so interested in it, I said, well, I may as well try to find out something or to go with him.
Remember that we, don't forget Marge that we were going to finish this off, but we had to put it off for the World Series you know. You've got to put first things first. (LAUGHTER).
Well now look, we are going to have to put another tape on, but we've got this connected up with ....... You had Louis at the Orchard Cabaret and now when do you play at the Cadillac?
Well, that was with Manuel Perez.
Oh!

That was after the, I don't know what happened after the Orchard. But I moved down to the Cadillac Café. That's just before I went into the Lyric Theater. And Albert Nicholas was playing clarinet. Lee Collins was on trumpet and Cozy Russell was on piano and myself on drums.
Yes, I'd forgotten Lee Collins.
He was from New Orleans too.
Yes. Sure.
He made that Nashville tour with us.
He was a good trumpet player even in those days wasn't he?
Yes, well he'd lose, he'd lose, he'd skip bars. He skipped probably a half a bar or maybe a bar. He could never keep that thing straight in his head.
Oh, that's a shame. Because he had a nice sound didn't he?
But he had a sound like Louis.
Yes, he could play so much like Louis.
Yes, he could.
When he was in Europe he used to break it up.
The only fault that I found with him, he'd get lost.
Is that so?
Yes. He'd skip bars it sounded like. He's thinking ahead you know.
Yes, yes. To what he was going to play?
Yes.
Yes, well that
That was the cause of him doing that missing those bars.
That's why he didn't go further than he did.
Oh man, the people in Europe just loved him.
Well I always thought he sounded great on those records. You know, those old records.
Yes, he sure did boy.
But then how long did this go at the Cadillac?
Well, it went on quite a while until old man Robichaux was standing outside listening at me play and that's how I got the job.
This is John Robichaux?
John. That's how, and Willie Jackson and Nooky would give me rehearsals on how the girls were going to kick and everything you know. Oh they had me really sharp and ready to go into the
Lyric Theater.
Where abouts was the Lyric Theater?
It was the Burgundy and, oh, Burgundy and, it was right on a corner. Burgundy and (Unintelligible).
Oh! Down in the Vieux Carre?

Yes. It was the next block, was the Palace Theater. That's where Ervin Le Claire and those guys were playing. And the drummer, Stein. He was a sensational drummer too. They shined the light on him. And that's what they used to do me at the Lyric, shine the light on me.
(REMAINDER OF FIRST TAPE ALMOST COMPLETELY INAUDIBLE. TYPIST DID NOT THINK WORTHWHILE TO TRY TO TRANSCRIBE).
* Lyric Theater - 201 Burgundy Street, viz - Rose & Souchon, New Orleans Jazz: A Family Album, p. 212 1967 ed.
